title: quick-start · Manual quick start (5 minutes)
text: In Ciaren, a saved pipeline is called a **flow** — you'll see that word everywhere in the editor and the API. This walkthrough uses the visual editor; an API-only version is at the bottom for developers who want to inspect the REST surface.

title: quick-start · Do I need an API key to use Ciaren?
text: No. Use the visual pipeline builder without an API key for a model provider. You can upload a CSV, connect nodes yourself, validate and run the flow locally, and export pandas or Polars code. A remote data service may require separate credentials if you choose its connector.

title: quick-start · What you'll build
text: By the end of this walkthrough you will have a running pipeline that cleans, aggregates, and outputs a summary CSV — plus the equivalent Python script.

title: quick-start · 1. Pick or Upload a Dataset
text: If you are using the Demo project, you can skip the upload and use an existing sample dataset.

title: quick-start · 1. Pick or Upload a Dataset
text: Ciaren infers the column schema and stores a sample. Datasets are **versioned** — re-uploading a file with the same name adds a new version rather than overwriting the old one, so existing flows stay reproducible.

title: quick-start · 3. Run the flow
text: Open the run from the **Runs** page to inspect each node and download the output.

title: quick-start · 4. Export Python
text: Click **Export**. Ciaren returns standalone, readable code for your flow, including **polars**, **pandas**, and **lazy polars** variants where available. Paste it into a script or a Jupyter notebook and it runs on its own, no Ciaren required.

title: quick-start · Prefer the API?
text: Everything above is also available over REST. The fastest way to explore it is the interactive docs at `http://localhost:8055/docs`.

title: engines · Engines: polars & pandas
text: Ciaren executes flows through a small **engine abstraction**, so the same visual flow runs on either **polars** or **pandas**. Every transformation node is engine-agnostic — it knows how to run on both and how to generate code for both.

title: engines · Which engine runs
text: polars is fast and memory-light on small-to-medium data; pandas is fully supported. You can change the server-wide default:

title: engines · Choosing an engine per run
text: A single run can override the default. In the UI, pick the engine when you run a flow; over the API, pass it in the run body:

title: engines · Choosing an engine per run
text: The chosen engine is **recorded on the run**, so the run is reproducible and you can see which engine produced a given output.

title: engines · Code export: pandas, polars, and lazy polars
text: Each input frame is named after its dataset file (`sales.csv` → `df_sales`) or SQL table, so the script talks about your data, not `df_1`. Steps on a straight chain fuse into one fluent method chain on a single variable, the way a person would write it, and blank lines separate the reads, each chain, and the writes. A step whose result feeds **several** later nodes (a fan-out, or a join input) keeps its own `df_N` variable, since it must stay alive for every consumer.

title: engines · Lazy polars (for large inputs)
text: The `polars (lazy)` variant reads with `scan_*` and builds a single **`LazyFrame`** query that only materializes at the final `collect()`. This lets polars apply projection and predicate pushdown (read fewer columns, filter at the scan) and optimize joins — a real speedup on large files for no change in results.

title: engines · Freeing intermediates (lower peak memory)
text: Pass `?free_intermediates=true` (the **Free intermediate tables (`del`)** checkbox in the export dialog) to add a `del` after each dataframe's last use in the pandas and eager-polars scripts. This releases intermediate tables sooner, lowering peak memory on long pipelines. A fully linear flow already reuses one variable throughout, so it has nothing to `del` — the option matters for flows with fan-outs or joins, where intermediates outlive the next step. The lazy script is unaffected — its variables are query plans, not materialized data, so there is nothing to free.

title: engines · Streaming reads at runtime (polars)
text: The above is about *exported code*. Inside Ciaren, the **polars** engine also loads CSV and Parquet inputs with a streaming reader (`scan_*` + a streaming `collect`), so a large input file is parsed in batches instead of all at once — lower peak memory at the point that usually dominates it. The result is identical to a plain read, so nothing else about your flow changes. (The pandas engine reads eagerly.)

title: engines · Execution mode: thread vs. process
text: Flow compute is synchronous (pandas/polars), so Ciaren runs it **off the event loop** to avoid blocking the API. `EXECUTION_MODE` selects how:

title: engines · Run timeouts
text: Each node also records a `duration_ms` in the run, so you can spot the slow step.

title: parameters · Flow Parameters
text: Parameters make a flow **reusable**: declare named, typed values once, reference them in any node field with `{{ name }}`, and supply different values each time you run, preview, schedule, or export the flow. Instead of one flow per file or per date, you keep a single flow and pass `{{ input_path }}` or `{{ run_date }}`.

title: parameters · Declaring parameters
text: In the flow editor, click **Parameters** in the top bar to open the parameter editor:

title: parameters · Declaring parameters
text: The button shows a badge with the number of declared parameters. Adding or editing parameters marks the flow **unsaved** — click **Save** to persist them (they're stored on the flow's graph, so they travel with import/export).

title: parameters · Referencing a parameter
text: Type `{{ name }}` into any node config field. When you select a node, the sidebar lists the available parameters as chips and warns if a field references a name you haven't declared.

title: parameters · Referencing a parameter
text: Bindings chosen from a dropdown — the dataset on an input node, or a connection — are **not** meant to be parameterized; pick those in the UI.

title: parameters · Supplying values
text: Precedence is **per-run override → per-schedule override → declared default**.

title: parameters · Running
text: Click **Run** on a flow that has parameters and a dialog opens, pre-filled with each parameter's default. Required parameters (no default) must be filled before the run can start. A blank optional field falls back to its default.

title: parameters · Scheduling
text: When you create or edit a schedule for a parameterized flow, the form shows a **Parameter values** section. Values entered there apply to **every** run the schedule fires; blanks fall back to defaults. This is how one flow backs several schedules that differ only by their parameter values.

title: parameters · Over the API
text: Pass a `parameters` object to the run endpoint:

title: parameters · Over the API
text: Unknown names, missing required values, and values that don't match the declared type are rejected with a `400` before the run starts. The resolved values are recorded on the run (visible on the run detail page) and re-used by **Retry**.

title: parameters · Previewing
text: The step preview in the editor uses each parameter's default, so what you preview matches what a default run would produce.

title: parameters · Exported code
text: Parameters become real variables at the top of the generated pandas and polars scripts, so the export is runnable as-is and easy to tweak:

title: parameters · Exported code
text: Whole-field references render as the bare variable (`df.head(keep)`); embedded references render as a `str.format` call (`'data/{}.csv'.format(run_date)`).

title: parameters · Tips & gotchas
text: Only reference a parameter inside one of these fields if every caller who can supply a run-time value (via the run API, a schedule, or your own app) is as trusted as the flow's author. If you're exposing "run this flow with end-user-supplied values" from your own application, don't let that untrusted input land in a script, expression, or SQL query field — put it in a plain filter/path/value field instead. :::

title: troubleshooting · Database connection fails
text: Ciaren uses async SQLAlchemy. A plain `sqlite://`, `postgresql://`, or `mysql://` URL will not connect. Use the async variant in `CIAREN_DATABASE_URL`:

title: troubleshooting · Frontend can't reach the backend
text: The dev server proxies `/api` to `http://localhost:8055` by default. If your backend runs elsewhere, point the proxy at it:

title: troubleshooting · Frontend can't reach the backend
text: If the frontend port `5173` is taken, change it with `VITE_PORT=3000 npm run dev` — and remember to add the new origin to `CIAREN_CORS_ORIGINS`.

title: troubleshooting · CORS errors
text: Add the calling origin to `CIAREN_CORS_ORIGINS` (a JSON list) in `backend/.env`:

title: troubleshooting · The assistant asks me to connect a provider
text: The flow assistant needs one enabled API key marked **In use**. Open **Connections → Assistant API keys**, add a key or select an existing one, and check that **Enabled** is on. Disabling or removing the key in use leaves none selected, and Ciaren does not pick another for you. If the server is configured through the environment instead, the key must be present and `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_ENABLED` must not be `false`. The status check never contacts the provider, so a configured key can still be rejected later.

title: troubleshooting · "Save your changes first" or "Proposal expired"
text: The assistant reads the saved flow, never the unsaved canvas. Choose **Save and send**, or save the canvas and send the request again. A proposal expires three minutes after it appears and cannot be applied if the flow, one of its input versions changed or the assistant was turned off in the meantime. Generate a new proposal. If another tab saved the flow, reload the editor and keep your local work first.

title: troubleshooting · "This model cannot edit flows" or a request is declined
text: Charts, machine learning and most multi-step flows need a model with tool calling. OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek models in the list qualify. The OpenCode models in the list do not, and use a smaller set of guided plans. Choose another key in **Connections**. Other replies are explanations, not errors: **The assistant was not confident** asks for a more specific request, **The proposal did not pass checks** means a draft failed validation and nothing was proposed, and **Too many steps for one request** means you should split the request into smaller changes. A draft marked **this draft was not checked** ran out of steps, time or provider connection, so review it with extra care.

title: troubleshooting · "Request budget used up"
text: Each application process allows 60 provider calls per rolling hour by default, and one complex Build can use up to 14. Wait for the window to pass, or raise `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_TURNS_PER_HOUR` and restart. "Another assistant turn is active" appears when eight requests are already running in the process, or the same request is repeated; wait a moment and send it again.

title: troubleshooting · Diagnose says there is no failed run
text: Diagnose explains the latest failed run of the flow. When a run succeeded but the result is wrong, such as rows missing after a Join, describe the change you want in **Build** instead. Diagnose proposes a fix only for an inner Join that drops left rows and for simple cleaning flows. For other failures it gives advice and asks for a manual edit.

title: troubleshooting · Upload rejected as too large
text: The default upload limit is 100 MB. Raise it with `CIAREN_MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB` in `backend/.env`.

title: troubleshooting · Module not found errors
text: Activate the environment you use to run Ciaren, then check whether the package is installed in that interpreter:

title: troubleshooting · Module not found errors
text: For a PyPI installation, run `python -m pip install ciaren` in that environment. For a source checkout, run `python -m pip install -e .` from the `backend/` directory instead. Using `python -m pip` keeps installation tied to the selected interpreter; a bare `pip` command can belong to a different environment.

title: troubleshooting · Install fails on Windows with a long-path error
text: A `pip install` can fail on Windows with an error like `OSError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '...\mlflow\store\db_migrations\versions\...'` and a hint about enabling *long-path support*. Ciaren bundles MLflow, whose internal file paths are long, so installing into a deeply nested folder can push the full path past Windows' legacy 260-character limit.

title: troubleshooting · ML training succeeds but the model isn't tracked (Windows)
text: A training run finishes **green**, its metrics show up, but the node's **model URI** and **MLflow run id** are blank — and a downstream **Predict** or **Feature Importance** node then fails because there's no model to load. The server log shows a warning like:

title: projects-and-runs · Projects & Runs
text: Beyond the editor, Ciaren helps you **organize** work and **monitor** what happened when a flow ran.

title: projects-and-runs · Projects
text: A **project** is a lightweight workspace that groups related datasets and flows.

title: projects-and-runs · Projects
text: You can scope dataset and flow listings to a project with `?project_id=...`.

title: projects-and-runs · Datasets
text: Upload CSV, TSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON/JSONL, or text files on the **Datasets** page. Ciaren infers a column schema and stores a small sample for previews.

title: projects-and-runs · Datasets
text: The **Profile** tab shows per-column statistics computed at upload time:

title: projects-and-runs · Dataset versioning
text: Datasets are **immutable and versioned**. Re-uploading a file under the same name appends a **new version** rather than overwriting the old one.

title: projects-and-runs · Runs
text: Every execution creates a **run** with its status, timestamps, logs, the engine used, and the resolved dataset versions. Browse them on the **Runs** page.

title: projects-and-runs · Run detail & per-node results
text: Opening a run (`/runs/:runId`) shows the flow as a read-only DAG. For each node it reports:

title: projects-and-runs · Run detail & per-node results
text: If a node fails, its error is captured and downstream nodes are marked `skipped`. Output files are only written when **every** node succeeds.

title: projects-and-runs · Cancelling a running run
text: A run that's still `running` can be stopped from its detail page, or via `POST /api/runs/{run_id}/cancel` (`202`). The executor checks for the request between nodes, so the in-flight node finishes and everything after it is marked `skipped`; the run ends with status `cancelled` and doesn't trigger a failure notification or count toward a schedule's auto-disable threshold. Cancelling a run that already finished returns `400`. In `process` execution mode, cancelling refuses (`400`) if another run is sharing the same worker pool, since recycling the pool would abort that other run too.

title: scheduling · Scheduling
text: Ciaren includes a lightweight, **in-process** scheduler that runs a flow automatically on a cron schedule — no broker, no extra services. It is meant for simple recurring jobs, not heavy orchestration; Ciaren is not an Airflow/dbt replacement.

title: scheduling · Creating a schedule
text: Click **Schedule** in the flow editor toolbar (or go to the **Schedules** page) to open the schedule builder:

title: scheduling · Creating a schedule
text: The frequency picker updates its human-readable summary and cron expression live as you switch between presets and Custom (cron). **Minutes** fires every N minutes (1-59) for sub-hourly cadences; **Hourly** fires once an hour at a chosen minute past:

title: scheduling · Creating a schedule
text: In the UI, open a flow (or the **Schedules** page) and add a schedule with a cron expression and timezone. Over the API:

title: scheduling · Creating a schedule
text: The UI includes a cron builder so you don't have to hand-write expressions.

title: docker · Docker
text: Ciaren ships a multi-stage Docker image that bundles the React frontend and the FastAPI backend into a single container. You get one port, one volume for data persistence, and zero Node.js or Python tooling required on the host.

title: docker · Image layout
text: The `/data` volume is the only path that changes at runtime. Mount it as a named volume (default) or a bind-mount to control where data lives on the host.

title: docker · Configuration
text: Every `CIAREN_*` setting can be passed as an environment variable. The `docker-compose.yml` already wires the most common ones through shell variables with sensible defaults, so you can override without editing the file:

title: docker · Configuration
text: Or create a `.env` file next to `docker-compose.yml`:

text: Extras are installed at **build time** via the `EXTRAS` build argument. Pass a comma-separated list:

title: docker · Optional feature extras
text: scikit-learn, MLflow, and joblib ship in every image — the ML nodes work with no extra. `EXTRAS` only adds:

title: docker · Data persistence
text: By default `docker-compose.yml` uses a named Docker volume (`ciaren-data`). All uploads, run outputs, the SQLite database, and MLflow run data live there.

title: docker · Data persistence
text: To use a **bind mount** instead (easier to inspect/backup):

title: docker · Image size notes
text: The image is built in two stages so no Node.js, npm, or build tooling ends up in the final layer:

title: docker · Image size notes
text: To further reduce size, avoid installing extras you don't need. The `ml` extra now only adds XGBoost and LightGBM, so its footprint is smaller than before — the base image itself is correspondingly larger since core ML libraries moved into it.

title: docker · Container exits immediately
text: Common causes: the `/data` directory isn't writable, or `DATABASE_URL` uses a sync driver. Check with `ciaren check` before starting.

title: docker · Health check fails
text: The container health check polls `/health` (liveness) every 30 seconds with a 60-second start period. If the server takes longer to start (e.g. due to a large migration), increase `start_period` in `docker-compose.yml`.

title: docker · Health check fails
text: For orchestrators (Kubernetes, a load balancer) use `/ready` as the **readiness** probe: it returns `503` until the database is reachable, so traffic is only routed once the instance can actually serve it. Keep `/health` as the liveness probe so a hung process is restarted without being masked by a transient DB blip.

title: docker · ML nodes not visible
text: The base image already includes scikit-learn, MLflow, and joblib, so the ML nodes only go missing if `CIAREN_ML_ENABLED=false` — or the image is somehow broken/stripped-down. XGBoost/LightGBM model *choices* specifically need the `ml` extra baked in at build time. Verify with:

title: docker · ML nodes not visible
text: A `[warn] ml: ...` line means either `CIAREN_ML_ENABLED` is off, or the image wasn't built normally — rebuild without a custom `--no-deps`-style override. Missing XGBoost/LightGBM specifically means rebuild with `EXTRAS=ml`.

text: The image only ships the `msodbcsql18` driver when built with `EXTRAS=mssql` (or `all-connectors`/`all`) — `unixodbc` alone is just the driver manager, with nothing registered in it. Rebuild with the extra:

title: connections · Assistant API keys
text: The top of the Connections page, above the data connections, is **Assistant API keys**. These are the provider keys the AI flow assistant uses to build flows from natural language. They are not database connections: no node uses them and flows never read them.

title: connections · Assistant API keys
text: Choose **Add API key**, name the key, pick the provider and a model, or choose **Other model…** to type a model ID that is not listed. Set a reasoning effort if the provider offers one, paste the key and confirm the storage notice. Ciaren stores the key in the OS keychain of the computer that runs it, which needs `ciaren[keyring]`, and never shows it again. The database keeps only the name, provider, model, effort and state.

title: connections · Assistant API keys
text: The assistant uses one enabled key at a time. The first key you add is in use, and you select another with its radio button. Clear **Enabled** to stop using a key without deleting it. The pencil button renames a key, changes its model or effort, or replaces the key, and the trash button deletes it from the keychain.

title: connections · Security model
text: A connection stores only a **secret reference** — never the value. Like Airflow's secrets backends, the reference picks where the secret lives; all sources are local, with no external service required:

title: connections · Security model
text: Whatever the source, the value is read only when a connection is used, and is:

title: connections · Security model
text: For an env var reference, set the variable before starting Ciaren:

title: connections · Security model
text: It's an extra (not part of the base install) so servers and containers stay lean, and it's pure-Python on every OS — no compiler needed. Then store a secret; the value is prompted, never echoed:

title: connections · Security model
text: and use `keyring:pg-main` as the connection's secret. `ciaren secret unset` removes it. :::

title: connections · Security model
text: You don't have to drop to the CLI, though: the connection form has a **"Store a value in the OS keychain"** button under the secret field. Enter a name and the value, click save, and Ciaren writes the value to the OS keychain and fills the field with the resulting `keyring:NAME` reference — the plaintext is sent once, stored only in the keychain, and never persisted, echoed back, or logged. When `ciaren[keyring]` isn't installed, or the host has no keychain daemon (headless servers, containers), the button stays visible but **disabled** and a hover explains what to install; `env:` or `file:` references apply there instead.

title: connections · Deleting a connection
text: Deleting a connection that flows still reference is refused with a message listing those flows — repoint their SQL/Storage nodes first, or force the delete (the UI asks; the API takes `?force=true`), after which those flows fail at run time until reconfigured.

title: connections · Supported databases
text: To pull in **every** database driver at once:

title: connections · Supported databases
text: Drivers are **optional**. If one isn't installed, that provider appears disabled on the Connections page with an "install …" hint, so the core stays lightweight. SQLite needs no driver and is great for trying things out.

title: connections · Creating a connection
text: The Connections page ships with two pre-seeded **built-in** connections you'll see before adding any of your own:

title: connections · Creating a connection
text: Both back core features out of the box and aren't meant to be deleted; treat them like defaults rather than connections you created.

title: connections · Creating a connection
text: SQLite asks only for a file path; most others ask for host, port, database, username, and the **password secret** — a reference (env var name, `keyring:NAME`, or `file:/path`), or use **Store a value in the OS keychain** to store the value in the OS keychain in place. The actual secret is never stored by Ciaren.

title: connections · Web APIs
text: The built-in **REST API** connector reads HTTP JSON/CSV endpoints like database tables — no driver required. It covers the connection options commercial tools offer:

title: connections · Web APIs
text: In a flow, use **SQL Input**: pick the API connection, then choose a declared **endpoint** or switch to **Custom request path** (e.g. `users?active=true`). Each run snapshots the response to parquet like any other input, so runs stay reproducible. API connections are **read-only** — SQL Output doesn't list them.

title: connections · Web APIs
text: The connector applies the same SSRF host guard as every other connector, and responses are size-capped before parsing — 256 MiB per request **and** cumulatively across the pages of one paginated read (with a hard ceiling of 1000 pages per read, whatever `max_pages` says). For larger extractions, filter or window the endpoint and split the read across runs.

title: connections · Reproducibility
text: Each run snapshots its SQL inputs to parquet, so a run records exactly the data it processed even though the source is live.

title: visualizations · Visualizations
text: While you build a flow, you can **chart the output of any node** without leaving the editor. Visualizations are for *inspection* — spotting distributions, outliers, trends, and relationships as you clean — not a pipeline output. They add nothing to the graph and are never written to a file.

title: visualizations · How to chart a node
text: The chart renders instantly. Switching chart type or columns is immediate — it re-draws from the data already loaded, so there's no waiting.

text: The picker groups chart types the same way this reference does:

text: This matters most for the **correlation heatmap**: a Pearson value on a sample can differ from the correlation over all the data. Treat the charts as a quick look for exploration, then run the flow to compute final results. :::

text: Most nodes have a single input handle (`in`) and a single output handle (`out`). Two nodes are different:

title: join · Join — `join`
text: Combine two inputs (`left`, `right`) on a key. Join is one of two multi-input nodes — connect one upstream node to its **left** handle and another to its **right** handle.

title: join · What it does
text: Join combines the **left** and **right** inputs on a shared key. The `how` parameter controls which rows survive — `inner` keeps only matches, `left` keeps all rows from the left input (filling nulls for unmatched right-side columns), `semi` keeps left rows with a match, and `anti` keeps left rows without a match. Semi and anti joins return only the left input's columns.

title: join · Configuration
text: Provide either `on` (same key name on both sides) **or** both `left_on` and `right_on` (different names).

title: join · Generated Python code
text: These exports left-join `df_1` and `df_2` on `customer_id`, preserving unmatched left rows and expanding duplicate right keys. pandas matches null keys in this join; Polars leaves them unmatched. Ciaren explicitly enables null matching for Polars semi/anti joins. Input names come from the two upstream exports.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Set up the Ciaren AI flow assistant and build a CSV flow
text: Use a four-row CSV to try the full cycle. You will describe a change in plain language, inspect the proposed nodes, save the flow, run it yourself and use its activity history to reverse the change.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Can Ciaren build a pipeline from a prompt?
text: Yes. Describe the result you want, and the assistant proposes real nodes, settings and connections for the whole flow: cleaning, joins, aggregations, date handling, data-quality checks, charts and, with the ML extension, features and models. You review the proposal and choose **Apply and save**, you choose when to run, and you can keep editing the flow by hand. The assistant works with your own API key from OpenAI, Anthropic or DeepSeek, and a model without tool calling gets a smaller set of guided plans.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Open an editor with Assistant
text: Open a flow and look for **Assistant** in the toolbar. The published 0.3.1 release predates this feature. If the button is missing, build from a source revision that includes the assistant. With Git, Python 3.12+, an activated virtual environment and Node 24.15 or later in the 24.x series, build the editor and install the local package:

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Open an editor with Assistant
text: Visit `http://127.0.0.1:8055`. The commands assume a new installation. For an existing database, back it up and run `ciaren db upgrade` before starting the upgraded server.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · How do I add a provider API key?
text: Until a key is in use, the assistant panel shows **Connect a provider** with an **Open connections** button. You can also open **Connections** and choose **Add API key** under **Assistant API keys**. Name the key, choose the provider and a model, or pick **Other model…** to type a model ID that is not listed. Paste the key, confirm the storage notice and choose **Save key**. Ciaren keeps the key in this computer's OS keychain, and the first key you add is the one the assistant uses. With several keys, select the one to use; only one is in use at a time.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Build a flow with a synthetic CSV
text: To build a flow, choose a project dataset on an empty canvas, describe the transformations and select **Create proposal**. The assistant generates the nodes and connections together. Review them before choosing **Apply and save**. **Run** executes the saved flow separately.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Build a flow with a synthetic CSV
text: The checks the assistant runs before you see a proposal use placeholder rows, so they confirm types and wiring, not your data. The run is where your real values are used.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Check the canvas and explain a node
text: Reload the editor page so the assistant panel returns to its opening screen. Open **Assistant**. The opening screen ends with a section marked **On device**. Choose **Check canvas** there to validate the wiring locally. Select a node on the canvas and choose **Explain selected node** to read its summary. Neither tool contacts a provider.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · How do I revert a saved change in activity history?
text: To revert a saved assistant change, open the flow’s **Assistant → Activity** history, choose **Show details** on the entry if you want to read it, and choose **Preview reversal**. Review the inverse, then choose **Confirm reversal**. Reload the flow to see both the original save and the reversal. On this example’s otherwise unchanged canvas the four added nodes disappear.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · How do I revert a saved change in activity history?
text: A reversal creates a new saved revision. The **Undo** button in the editor toolbar changes your local canvas instead. Save or discard pending edits before previewing a reversal. If another editor changes a setting involved in the reversal, keep your local work, compare the saved version and review a fresh preview. Reversing a flow does not run it or remove earlier run results.

title: flow-assistant-quick-start · Change a flow you already have
text: On a flow that already has nodes, keep **Build** selected and describe the change, for example “Sort the amounts from high to low before the output.” The assistant sees the node types and connections of the canvas but not their current settings, so say what should change. The proposal lists the nodes it adds or updates and the connections it changes. The assistant can add nodes and change settings and connections, but it does not delete nodes that were already on the canvas. Remove those yourself.

title: flow-assistant · Flow assistant for visual ETL
text: Describe the data flow you want in plain language. The assistant proposes the nodes, settings and connections for the canvas, checks the result and shows it to you for review. Nothing is saved until you choose **Apply and save**, nothing runs until you choose **Run**, and you can keep editing the flow by hand at any point.

title: flow-assistant · Flow assistant for visual ETL
text: The assistant is bring-your-own-key and starts off. Add a provider API key under **Connections → Assistant API keys** to turn it on. ChatGPT and Claude consumer subscriptions have separate billing from their APIs. It is an alpha feature: review every proposal, because the assistant's own checks confirm types and wiring, not that your data produces the result you want.

title: flow-assistant · What you can ask for
text: With OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek or a model you type that supports tool calling, Build works step by step. The assistant looks up node settings in the installed catalog, reads the column types of your datasets, drafts edits, checks the flow and corrects its own mistakes before it shows you one proposal. You can describe a whole pipeline in a single request, in any language, up to 1,500 characters.

title: flow-assistant · What you can ask for
text: These requests use only nodes the assistant can create. Replace the column names with your own.

title: flow-assistant · What you can ask for
text: The panel offers a few starting prompts under **Try**, based on the selected dataset. Results depend on the model you choose, so treat the first proposal as a draft: send a clearer request, choose **Regenerate**, or fix the details by hand after saving.

title: flow-assistant · What you can ask for
text: Two things help the assistant most. Name the columns you mean, because it does not see your column names unless you share them. When it cannot tell which column you meant, it asks. And describe what to change on an existing flow, because the assistant sees the node types and connections of the canvas but not the current settings of its nodes.

title: flow-assistant · Build, review and apply
text: The assistant works from the saved flow. While the canvas has unsaved edits, the toolbar **Save** button carries a small dot. If you send a request before saving, the request stays in the box, **Save** pulses briefly and **Save and send** saves the canvas and sends the request.

title: flow-assistant · What a proposal shows
text: A proposal opens with a one-sentence summary and up to four short notes. A map of the flow follows, then every added or updated node with its settings. Each updated node lists every setting that changes, and **All settings** lists every field of a new node. Expand **Connections** to check the ports, or **Compare all settings** to inspect an existing node. **Inspect on canvas** returns to that node, and updated nodes are highlighted on the canvas while the proposal is open. Expression nodes show the whole expression, so you can read it before saving. **Steps** lists what the assistant did, such as reading dataset columns, drafting a change and checking the flow, and a line below shows the provider calls and tokens the request used.

title: flow-assistant · What a proposal shows
text: A proposal expires after three minutes. A draft that ran out of steps or time, or lost the provider, carries a note that it was not checked. Read such a draft with extra care, or regenerate it.

title: flow-assistant · What a proposal shows
text: After **Apply and save**, a message offers **Undo** for about 12 seconds. Undo reverses that saved change as a new revision, the same as a reversal in Activity, and works only while the canvas still matches what was saved. Later, reverse the change from Activity.

title: flow-assistant · When it asks a question
text: When a request leaves a real choice open, the reply is a card with one button per option instead of a proposal. A common case is a request that describes columns the types cannot identify. The buttons show your real column names, and choosing one sends the pick back as a column reference, so the name still stays on the server. A request can carry up to three answers. If no option fits, edit the request with more detail. When the assistant cannot offer options, the reply offers **Share column names and retry**.

title: flow-assistant · While it works
text: A request keeps running while the panel is closed, and the **Assistant** button shows a dot when the reply is ready. **Cancel request** stops the request and closes the provider connection, and so does leaving the flow. A provider can still bill work already performed. A saved-flow revision conflict, a changed input version or an expired proposal requires a new proposal. Reload the editor after a concurrent save, preserving any local work first. A reply can end with buttons for a likely next step, such as saving, sharing column names or opening a guide.

title: flow-assistant · What the assistant can build
text: The assistant can use these built-in nodes:

title: flow-assistant · What the assistant can build
text: Filter Expression, Calculated Column and Assert Expression accept a short arithmetic or comparison expression such as `price * qty > 100`. The server allows only column references, numbers, single-quoted text, comparison and arithmetic operators and the functions `abs`, `sqrt`, `exp`, `log10`, `log1p`, `sin`, `cos`, `floor` and `ceil`. The proposal highlights these nodes so you can read the expression before saving.

title: flow-assistant · What the assistant can build
text: On an existing flow the assistant can add nodes, change the settings of nodes of these types and rewire connections. It cannot delete a node that was already on the canvas, so remove those yourself. Nodes of any other type stay as they are, and the assistant can neither edit them nor connect to them.

title: flow-assistant · What the assistant can build
text: The assistant never writes Python Transform nodes, database or cloud storage connectors, format-specific outputs, forecasting models or plugin nodes. It cannot change credentials or file paths. Model settings are limited to the documented hyperparameters with upper bounds, for example at most 500 trees and 20 cross-validation folds. A request that needs anything else ends with an explanation instead of a partial flow. Add those nodes in the editor.

title: flow-assistant · What the assistant can build
text: The assistant edits canvases of up to 80 nodes and 160 connections, and reads at most 64 columns of each dataset. It can use the datasets you select in the panel and those already on the canvas.

title: flow-assistant · How the assistant checks its work
text: The checks run on placeholder rows: each input keeps its column names, types, row count (up to 200 rows), distinct-value counts and whether a column has nulls, but every value is generated. Types and wiring are checked before you see the proposal. A value-dependent failure, such as text that does not parse as a date, appears when you run the flow, and **Diagnose** can then look at it. Data-quality nodes such as Assert Row Count pass their rows through in these checks and run when you run the flow.

title: flow-assistant · How the assistant checks its work
text: Columns named after values, such as one-hot or pivot columns, have generated names in these checks, so the assistant cannot select them by name. A model node then uses every column except the target.

title: flow-assistant · Models without tool calling
text: The OpenCode models in the list below have no tool calling. With them, Build uses guided plans instead: up to six basic cleaning steps (limit, sort, drop nulls, remove duplicates, select or drop columns and filter), the two-input Join and the shipping regression below. A request for charts, models or other nodes is declined with a suggestion to choose a model with tool calling or to edit the canvas, or it returns no change. A model you type is assumed to support tool calling.

title: flow-assistant · Join two datasets
text: On an empty canvas select the left dataset, then the optional **Right input for Join**. Both must belong to the flow's project, and the right input appears only when both datasets are CSV files. With a tool-calling model, describe the join in your own words. The assistant chooses the key from the columns and builds the rest of the flow.

title: flow-assistant · Join two datasets
text: With a model that has no tool calling, Ciaren uses a fixed Join plan. Both CSVs need one same-named key of the same type within the first 64 columns of each input and no other overlapping column names. Open **Data shared with provider** and choose **Include column names in this request** if the question refers to specific fields. Review the two filenames, versions, key, join mode and left/right wiring before applying.

title: flow-assistant · Join two datasets
text: A guided Join can keep matching rows (`inner`) or retain all left rows (`left`), add one boolean equality flag on a text column, sort ascending by one input column and write a CSV. For the repository's `examples/orders-audit`, choose orders on the left and catalog on the right. Ask to keep all orders by SKU, mark `ready_to_fulfill` when `catalog_status` equals `active`, and sort by `order_id`. The flag uses Ciaren's built-in Conditional Column.

title: flow-assistant · Join two datasets
text: Duplicate keys can multiply rows. With null keys on both sides, pandas can match the nulls while Polars leaves them unmatched.

title: flow-assistant · Walkthrough: recover a missing order
text: Diagnose is for runs that failed. When the latest run succeeded but rows are missing, describe the repair in Build as above. The recording uses the packaged editor, the synthetic orders audit and a simulated provider response. The canvas, validation, saves and history use the real application.

title: flow-assistant · Train a shipping cost model from three CSVs
text: With the ML extension enabled, Build can generate a fixed regression plan from three CSVs: two inner joins followed by a seeded train/test split, linear regression, held-out prediction, evaluation and a metrics CSV. It works with any provider, including models without tool calling. This plan starts on an empty canvas. The first CSV supplies the numeric target, and each lookup contributes one numeric predictor. Identifiers used for joining cannot be training features or targets. With a tool-calling model you can also describe a different training flow in your own words, as in the examples above.

title: flow-assistant · Train a shipping cost model from three CSVs
text: Each lookup must have exactly one compatible key in common with the first CSV. The lookups must have distinct column names from each other. Ciaren checks the saved profile for a unique, non-null key across the whole lookup. A sampled profile cannot establish uniqueness. Both joins keep matched rows. The run needs at least 13 matching orders with usable numeric targets. The provider receives no rows or key values, so the proposal cannot establish how many orders match. Review the run counts when using your own data.

title: flow-assistant · Train a shipping cost model from three CSVs
text: The split uses seed 42 and holds out 20% of matched rows. Only the training branch fits the model. Choose features available at prediction time. Repeated measurements or historical forecasts can need a grouped or time-based split in a manually built flow. The three selected dataset versions and the flow revision are checked again before saving.

title: flow-assistant · Train a shipping cost model from three CSVs
text: On **Run**, the existing training node logs the fitted model and up to five rows of feature values to the installation’s configured MLflow store. That store can be remote. The LLM receives only the request and temporary join, target and predictor references by default. Opting in shares column names for that turn. When a lookup has multiple numeric candidates, Ciaren requires the opt-in to distinguish them. The model cannot choose a tracking endpoint, model URI, arbitrary hyperparameters or executable code.

title: flow-assistant · Activity and reversal
text: Open **Assistant → Activity** to see confirmed changes for this flow, most recent first. Entries read **Proposal saved**, **Repair saved** or **Reversal**. Expand **Show details** to see node types, ports and fields, including the before and after for supported settings. Proposals, requests, provider responses, key material, rows and full graph snapshots are excluded. Activity starts with the first assistant save after upgrading. Run `ciaren db upgrade` on existing installations before starting the upgraded server. On MySQL and MariaDB the migration enables microsecond precision on flow revisions.

title: flow-assistant · Activity and reversal
text: Reversals preserve unrelated edits when the saved inverse can be proven safe. For example, reverting a Join mode keeps a later downstream sort. Ciaren checks the project, flow revision, affected settings, dependencies and bound inputs again when you confirm. If another client saves after a preview, preserve local work, reload and preview again. A changed dependency, a removed input, or a prior private value that cannot be reconstructed requires a manual edit. Reversals are final entries in the timeline; a fresh proposal can reapply a change.

title: flow-assistant · Activity and reversal
text: The editor sends the loaded revision on **Save** and on the save before **Run**. Run creation checks the returned revision again before taking its execution snapshot. If you edit during a Run, the editor keeps the draft open and links to the result. A conflict leaves the draft on the canvas and offers a separate tab to compare the saved version. API callers can pass `expected_revision` (the flow’s `updated_at`) on both `PUT /api/flows/{id}` and `POST /api/flows/{id}/runs`. Older clients that omit it retain unconditional save and latest-version execution; upgrade those clients to protect their writes.

title: flow-assistant · Activity and reversal
text: Access follows the installation’s existing server authentication. The timeline records the source of a change and the user’s confirmation without attributing it to a named person. A moved flow’s prior project entries are hidden. Activity pages contain up to 20 entries. Reversal previews use up to 64 short-lived process-local references with a three-minute timeout. Use sticky routing or a single process for confirmations. Deleting the flow deletes its activity.

title: flow-assistant · What leaves the server
text: Every request includes the text you enter. Keep credentials and confidential row values out of that text. A column name you type in a request is matched to its column, and the model receives that name only as part of your text plus a reference for the column.

title: flow-assistant · What leaves the server
text: By default the model receives these facts about a Build request:

title: flow-assistant · What leaves the server
text: Other column names reach the provider only when you opt in for a single request with **Include column names in this request**. The option also sends the names of derived columns in the check results. A Join repair sends the question, a temporary Join reference, its current mode and, during diagnosis, a fixed error category. The shipping regression sends temporary join, target and predictor references. Documentation questions send up to five bundled passages without canvas context.

title: flow-assistant · What leaves the server
text: Files, samples, row values, filenames, dataset IDs, connection details, node labels, scripts, full configuration, raw logs and error traces stay on the server. Replies shown in the panel use the names you see in the editor, never internal references. Recommendations and citations are rendered as text. Because no check reads real values, its outcome cannot answer a guess about your data, for example whether a filter matches any row.

title: flow-assistant · What leaves the server
text: The assistant cannot run a pipeline. Review uses ordinary Ciaren nodes, so the existing run, export and undo controls continue to work.

title: flow-assistant · Deployment and credentials
text: Ciaren settings and provider credentials belong to one server instance. Anyone with access to its API can manage the assistant within the installation's token and browser-origin rules. Deploy separate instances, data directories and secret sources for separate trust boundaries. Use TLS and the Ciaren API token for a networked installation. Configure reverse proxies and monitoring to omit request bodies and authorization headers. Restrict process and diagnostic dump access at the operating-system level.

title: flow-assistant · Keys on the Connections page
text: Choose **Add API key** under **Connections → Assistant API keys**. Name the key, pick the provider and a model from the list, or choose **Other model…** and type the provider's exact model ID. Typed models are not tested with Ciaren. They use tool calling, so a model without it fails with a provider error. Set a reasoning effort when the provider offers one. Read the storage notice and confirm it before you save.

title: flow-assistant · Keys on the Connections page
text: Ciaren saves the key in the OS keychain of the computer that runs it: Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain or Secret Service. Install `ciaren[keyring]` and keep the keychain unlocked. **Add API key** stays disabled, with a note, on a computer where Ciaren finds no supported keychain, such as a headless server or container. Use the server-managed keys below there. Entries use a separate service derived from the resolved data directory. The database stores only the name, provider, model, effort and state, and Ciaren never shows a saved key again.

title: flow-assistant · Keys on the Connections page
text: The assistant uses one key at a time. The first key you add becomes the one in use. To switch, select another enabled key. Clear **Enabled** to stop using a key without removing it. A disabled key cannot be selected, and disabling the key in use leaves none selected until you pick one. Use the pencil button to rename a key, change its model or effort, or replace the key. A replacement asks for the storage notice again. The provider of a saved key is fixed. **Remove** deletes the key from the keychain.

title: flow-assistant · Keys on the Connections page
text: Anyone who can use this Ciaren server can run the assistant with the key in use, on your bill. Prefer a key with a spending limit.

title: flow-assistant · Server-managed keys
text: Without a selected key, an operator can configure the assistant in the server environment. Set `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER` to `openai`, `anthropic`, `deepseek`, `opencode` or `off`. Set provider-specific variables such as `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_OPENAI_MODEL` and `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_OPENAI_EFFORT`. Use the provider name in capitals. The model must be one of the listed models. Only OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek expose an `_EFFORT` variable. For a direct DeepSeek API key, use `deepseek` and `deepseek-flash`. An OpenCode Go credential belongs to OpenCode. This version’s OpenCode adapter has no DeepSeek model. A key selected on the Connections page takes precedence. Set `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_ENABLED=false` and restart to turn the assistant off on the server, including saved keys.

title: flow-assistant · Server-managed keys
text: For Docker or a headless install, set the non-secret variables below and mount the selected secret file. Keep the source file outside the repository, build context, data directory and connector roots. Set `CIAREN_STORAGE_ALLOWED_ROOTS` to dedicated dataset folders on shared installations.

title: flow-assistant · Server-managed keys
text: For the repository Compose setup, save the fragment as `docker-compose.override.yml` alongside `docker-compose.yml`. Set the host path to an existing secret file and recreate the service with `docker compose up -d --build ciaren`. For process injection, set `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_DEEPSEEK_KEY_SOURCE=env` and have your secret manager supply `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` to the server process when using DeepSeek. Keep secrets out of shell history and committed environment files.

title: flow-assistant · Server-managed keys
text: Revoke compromised keys in the provider console as well. Status checks do not contact the provider. A configured status means Ciaren found the key, not that the provider accepts it.

title: flow-assistant · Bounds and implementation
text: Input is limited to 1,500 request characters, 80 canvas nodes, 160 edges and 64 columns per source. One Build turn makes at most 14 provider calls and 40 tool calls within 120 seconds. Each provider call has a 35-second timeout, 4,096 output tokens and a 48 KB request limit, and each tool call 15 seconds. The opening request is at most 12 KB, and older tool results are compacted to keep each call within its limit. One edit applies up to 24 operations. Each check previews at most 50,000 rows and 2 million cells per node within 15 seconds; a single slow node step can overrun that deadline. Up to eight turns may be active per process. Up to 64 proposals live in memory for three minutes. Use a single process or sticky routing for proposal confirmation.

title: flow-assistant · Bounds and implementation
text: Each application process allows 60 provider calls per rolling hour by default (`CIAREN_ASSISTANT_TURNS_PER_HOUR`). The limit counts calls, not turns: a turn reserves its calls when it starts and returns the unused ones when it ends. A complex Build can use all 14, so the default allows about four of them an hour; raise the limit if you need more. Set `CIAREN_ASSISTANT_TOKENS_PER_HOUR` to also cap tokens. Configure provider-side spend limits for a currency-denominated cap. Requests use zero automatic retries. If a turn reaches its call limit, the assistant validates the latest draft and returns it when it passes, or returns it flagged as unchecked. The UI renders a change only after the server has validated its operations; review an unchecked draft before applying it. Cancelling a turn does not return its reserved calls.

title: flow-assistant · Bounds and implementation
text: The tools run inside the Ciaren server against the installed node registry and the same validation as the editor. The model receives turn-local references (`d0` for datasets, `n0` for nodes, `c0` for columns), never dataset IDs, file paths or rows. Every edit passes an allowlist of node types and settings before anything runs, and nothing is saved until you choose **Apply and save**. In Build, nodes of types outside the allowlist, such as plugin, code and connector nodes, stay locked. In Diagnose, flows that contain them receive read-only recommendations based on node types, wiring and the failure category. Edit those nodes in the regular editor.

title: external-agent · Does Ciaren provide an MCP server?
text: Ciaren does not ship a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a stdio command for MCP clients or an MCP registration URL. The editor's Flow Assistant calls tools inside the Ciaren server through the provider's function calling. Its provider key is managed under **Connections → Assistant API keys**, or by the server environment, and applies only to that editor feature.

title: external-agent · Does Ciaren provide an MCP server?
text: For an agent you maintain, the supported integration interfaces are the Ciaren REST API and the Python SDK. A small catalog lookup lets an agent answer a question about the installed nodes without reading a dataset or executing a pipeline.

title: external-agent · Give an agent one read-only lookup
text: Start your local Ciaren server with `ciaren serve`. Install the client from the same checkout with `python -m pip install ./client`. Save this as `join_ports.py` and run `python join_ports.py`:

title: external-agent · Give an agent one read-only lookup
text: The expected result is `['left', 'right']`. Register only this fixed function with your own agent host. It calls `GET /api/catalog/nodes` and returns two port IDs. This lookup works with the editor assistant switched off and needs no model provider or provider key.

title: external-agent · Give an agent one read-only lookup
text: If your installation requires authentication, supply the Ciaren server token to the host process via its environment. Keep it out of prompts and tool results. The installation token can authorize other operations; the fixed function limits what this particular tool exposes. Keep writes, arbitrary requests and run submission outside that tool. The editor’s proposal review and Activity history apply to the built-in assistant.
